kurals.tamil:
பல்லார் முனியப் பயனில சொல்லுவான்
எல்லாரும் எள்ளப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pallaar muniyap payanila solluvaan,
Ellaarum ellap padum.
kurals.meaning: A person who keeps pouring out useless talk until many listeners are fed up with him ends up being looked down on by everyone.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone in class who keeps talking and talking about nothing while everyone is trying to listen to the teacher. Soon nobody wants to sit next to them. This kural says that people who chatter about useless things make everyone tired of them, and then everyone stops respecting them.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with a social rather than a metaphysical sanction: the idle talker is punished by the listening community itself. The verb முனிய (muniya, “to be vexed, to loathe”) names the listeners’ reaction, and எள்ளப்படும் (ellappadum, “will be scorned”) names the outcome, so the couplet traces a causal chain from speech to irritation to contempt. The contrast of பல்லார் (“the many” who hear him) with எல்லாரும் (“everyone”) is deliberate: annoyance starts with the immediate audience but reputation spreads to the whole world. Coming straight after the chapter on backbiting (புறங்கூறாமை), the kural widens the ethics of speech from malicious words to merely empty ones, treating wasted words as a real, if quieter, wrong. Plutarch’s essay on garrulousness makes the same diagnosis, that the chatterer seeks affection and wins hatred.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him not seek after many words, for that is mere weariness of the tongue.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad tells the seeker who has found the Self to practise wisdom instead of piling up words, which only tire the tongue.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat piling up words as fruitless. The Kural stresses how it wears on the listeners, and the Upanishad how it wears out the speaker.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad IV.4.21 (trans. F. Max Müller, SBE 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shared distrust of many words, but the Upanishad’s context is spiritual practice, not social contempt for a babbler.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself. … A fool also is full of words.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher contrasts gracious speech with a fool’s endless words, which end up destroying the fool himself.
christianity.tie_back: In both texts the babbler is the one who pays: the Kural’s talker ends up scorned, and the Preacher’s fool is swallowed by his own lips.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on the self-harm of a ‘full of words’ fool; the Kural’s specific mechanism (the many grow vexed) is only implied.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah has hated for you three things: -1. Vain talks, (useless talk) that you talk too much or about others.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet lists qīla wa qāla (‘it was said and he said’, meaning idle chatter) first among three things God dislikes for people.
islam.tie_back: In the Kural the whole world scorns the idle talker, and in the hadith God himself dislikes idle talk. Both condemn it plainly.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct condemnation of idle talk; the hadith grounds the aversion in God rather than in public scorn.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that useth many words shall be abhorred; and he that taketh to himself authority therein shall be hated.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Sira, a Second-Temple Jewish sage, warns that the person who talks too much will be loathed by those around him.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own claim: too many words lead to being abhorred, just as the Kural’s talker is scorned by all.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match. Ben Sira is outside the Hebrew canon but is ancient Jewish wisdom quoted in rabbinic literature.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “They blame those who remain silent, they blame those who speak much, they blame those who speak in moderation. There is none in the world who is not blamed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Atula that people criticise everyone, including those who talk too much.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say that the heavy talker is criticised. The Buddha, however, adds that the silent are blamed too, which softens the Kural’s sharp contrast.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Partial match only: the verse’s real point is that blame is universal, not that babbling specifically earns contempt.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A man of many words, and those unseemly; a monger of sedition, a railer against all who were in authority, who cared not what he said, so that he might set the Achaeans in a laugh.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Thersites harangues the Greek assembly at Troy. The soldiers are ‘angry and disgusted’, and when Odysseus beats him, the whole army laughs at him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural in narrative form: a man whose many words disgust the many is scorned by all.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close: disgust of the assembly followed by universal derision. Thersites’ speech is abusive as well as idle.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In the case of babblers … they are hated when they wish to be liked, that they cause annoyance when they wish to please, that they are laughed at when they think they are admired.”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch diagnoses garrulousness as a disease whose sufferers get the opposite of what they want from their audience.
philosophy.tie_back: Plutarch’s babbler, like the Kural’s, annoys his listeners and is despised by them.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On Talkativeness (De garrulitate) 16, 510c-d (trans. W. C. Helmbold, Loeb)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel of cause (annoying the many) and effect (being hated and laughed at).

kurals.tamil:
பயனில பல்லார்முன் சொல்லல் நயனில
நட்டார்கண் செய்தலிற் றீது.
kurals.transliteration:
Payanila pallaarmun sollal nayanila,
Nattaarkan seydhalir reedhu.
kurals.meaning: Talking pointless nonsense in front of many people is worse than doing unkind things to your own friends.
kurals.elementary: If you are rude to one friend, that hurts one person. But if you stand up in front of the whole school and waste everyone’s time with silly talk, you hurt everyone’s time at once. This kural says doing that in front of many people is even worse than being unkind to a friend.
kurals.university: The couplet works through a startling comparison. Doing நயனில (nayanila, “what is devoid of goodness/propriety”) to நட்டார் (nattaar, “friends”), which is a real ethical fault, is ranked below speaking பயனில (payanila, “what is devoid of benefit”) before பல்லார் (“the many”). The two phrases rhyme (nayanila / payanila), and the parallel sound makes the ranking stick in the ear. The argument depends on scale and publicity: an unkind act toward a friend stays in a private relationship that can be repaired, while empty talk before an assembly wastes the attention of many people at once and fixes one’s public character. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all keep this ‘worse than’ reading, which shows how seriously Valluvar takes the public squandering of speech.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrihari’s Nītiśataka calls silence the ornament that the unlearned can wear in an assembly of the wise, a covering for their lack of knowledge.
hinduism.explanation: The gnomic poet advises that in a learned gathering the unqualified are better off saying nothing than exposing themselves.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts see the assembly as the place where empty talk does the most damage, and both advise silence there.
hinduism.source: Bhartrihari, Nītiśataka (verse on silence as the ornament of the unlearned; numbering varies by edition)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; shares the ‘before many’ setting but makes no comparison with harming friends.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that even ‘idle’ (argos, workless) words are weighed at the final judgment.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts insist that careless words weigh more than people assume. The Kural ranks them above unkind deeds, and Jesus makes them answerable before God.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on the gravity of idle words; lacks the Kural’s specific comparison with wronging friends.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [they are] those who do not testify to falsehood, and when they pass near ill speech, they pass by with dignity.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes God’s true servants as refusing to join in laghw (vain, idle speech) when they come across it.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link dignity with keeping out of vain talk when others are present.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear stance against vain talk, but no ranking against harming friends.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If two sit together and there are no words of Torah [spoken] between them, then this is a session of scorners.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradion says that a gathering filled only with empty talk turns into a ‘seat of the scornful’.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts judge talk by its social setting: empty words in company harm the whole gathering.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:2 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit on corrupted company; the Mishnah measures talk against Torah, not against ‘benefit’ in general.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It isn’t right, monks, that sons of good families, on having gone forth out of faith from home to the homeless life, should get engaged in such topics of conversation.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha finds monks gathered in the assembly hall chatting about kings, food, gossip and so on, and tells them to discuss ten wholesome topics instead.
buddhism.tie_back: Here idle talk in an assembly is corrected at once, which reflects the Kural’s concern about pointless words before many.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 10.69, Kathavatthu Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close in setting (a group gathering) and judgment; no explicit comparison with harming friends.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, the mortal favoured with a seat at the gods’ table, falls by an ‘unbridled tongue’ in Euripides’ telling: he betrays the confidences of his divine hosts by talking.
greek_mythology.explanation: Several versions put Tantalus’s crime in his mouth (leaking the gods’ secrets) rather than in a deed, and he suffers eternal punishment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Tantalus tradition, like the Kural, rates reckless speech as worse than a wrong done by hand to one’s friends.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Orestes 4-10 (the ‘unbridled tongue’ of Tantalus); cf. Pindar, Olympian 1
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Other versions blame a deed (serving Pelops), and his fault is indiscreet speech, not merely idle speech.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Theophrastus’s sketch of ‘The Garrulous Man’ shows a man who sits beside strangers and pours out his dreams, dinners and trivial opinions to anyone within earshot.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle’s successor catalogues the chatterer as a recognisable social type whose talk burdens every company he enters.
philosophy.tie_back: Theophrastus shows how public idle talk imposes on many people at once, which is why the Kural judges it so harshly.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a portrait; shows the public nuisance but makes no ranking against wronging friends.

kurals.tamil:
நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும் பயனில
பாரித் துரைக்கும் உரை.
kurals.transliteration:
Nayanilan enbadhu sollum payanila,
Paarith thuraikkum urai.
kurals.meaning: When a man spreads out long talk about worthless things, that talk itself announces to the world that he lacks goodness.
kurals.elementary: You can often tell what kind of person someone is just by listening to them. If a person keeps talking on and on about useless things, their own words are like a sign on their back that says, “I am not a good person.” They don’t even need anyone else to say it.
kurals.university: The grammar is striking: the subject of சொல்லும் (“will declare”) is the talk itself (உரை, urai), so speech bears witness against the speaker. பாரித்து (paarittu, “spreading out, amplifying”) condemns not a single slip but the habit of stretching trivial matter into long discourse. The key term நயனிலன் (nayanilan, “one without nayan”) is glossed differently by modern commentators: Mu. Varadarasan reads it as lacking virtue (aram), Solomon Pappaiah as lacking justice (neethi), and Kalaignar as simply a ‘useless person’. All of these readings agree that speech works as a public index of inner character. The same idea appears in Solon’s maxim that speech is the image of actions, and in the Buddha’s teaching that discernment is revealed through conversation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Keshav, what is the disposition of one who is situated in divine consciousness? How does an enlightened person talk? How does he sit? How does he walk?”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna asks how inner realisation shows outwardly, and the first sign he asks about is speech.
hinduism.tie_back: Both assume that speech shows a person’s inner state. The Kural uses the idea negatively (empty talk exposes a lack of virtue), and the Gita positively.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the premise that speech reveals character; the Gita frames it as a question about the sage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool’s voice is known by multitude of words.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher says a fool can be recognised by the sheer quantity of his words.
christianity.tie_back: In both texts, piling up empty words identifies the kind of person who speaks them.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: too many words work as a diagnostic sign of character.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed among the excellence of a person’s Islam is that he leaves what does not concern him.”
islam.explanation: This widely taught saying (also no. 12 in al-Nawawi’s Forty Hadith) makes leaving aside irrelevant matters, including irrelevant talk, a measure of how good someone’s faith is.
islam.tie_back: Both texts read engagement with trivial matters as a measure of inner quality.
islam._accuracy_note: Good conceptual match. Darussalam grades this particular chain da’if, though the saying is widely accepted via other routes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A small coin in an empty barrel calls: Kish, kish.”
judaism.explanation: Ulla quotes a folk proverb: one coin in an empty jar rattles loudly, while a full jar makes no noise. (The words ‘small’ and ‘empty’ are the translator’s clarifying additions.)
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say that noisy talk shows inner emptiness.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 85b (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz trans., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong image-level match; in the Talmud it describes a scholar among ignorant kin, a slightly different context.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It’s through discussion that a person’s discernment may be known, and then only after a long period, not a short period.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a small fish can be told from the ripples it makes, and in the same way a dull mind can be told from how a person talks.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts treat speech as the window through which others read what a person is like inside.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.192, Thana Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Clear parallel of speech-as-evidence; the sutta measures discernment rather than virtue.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Oho, my friend, it’s you, is it? I, too, should have been afraid if I hadn’t heard your voice.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aesop’s fable an ass dressed in a lion’s skin scares everyone until he brays, and the fox recognises him at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Speech gives the speaker away. In the Kural, empty talk exposes a man without worth just as the bray exposes the ass.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, ‘The Ass in the Lion’s Skin’ (trans. V. S. Vernon Jones, 1912)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Aesopic fable rather than myth proper; very close on ‘speech betrays the speaker’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He used to say, too, that speech was the image of actions.”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes Laertius records Solon’s maxim that a man’s words mirror his deeds and character.
philosophy.tie_back: Solon’s ‘speech is the image’ is the Kural’s point in general terms: empty speech reflects an empty moral life.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 1.58 (Solon) (trans. C. D. Yonge)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good general parallel; Solon does not single out idle speech.

kurals.tamil:
நயன்சாரா நன்மையின் நீக்கும் பயன்சாராப்
பண்பில்சொல் பல்லா ரகத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Nayansaaraa nanmaiyin neekkum payansaaraap,
Panbilsol pallaa rakaththu.
kurals.meaning: Words that bring no benefit and have no refinement, spoken among many people, cut a person off from virtue and remove him from goodness.
kurals.elementary: Think of a garden. Every time you throw rubbish into it, the flowers have less room to grow. Rude, useless talk in front of others is like throwing rubbish into your own heart’s garden. Bit by bit, it pushes the good things out.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on two paired negatives, பயன்சாரா (“not joined to benefit”) and நயன்சாரா (“not joined to nayan”, i.e., virtue or propriety), with பண்பில் (panpil, “uncultured, graceless”) in between. The claim is about moral formation, not reputation: such speech நன்மையின் நீக்கும் (“removes one from goodness”), gradually alienating the speaker from his own better character. Mu. Varadarasan reads the result as ‘not joining with aram and being removed from good’, while Kalaignar stresses that it also destroys the listeners’ pleasure. The setting பல்லாரகத்து (“among many”) again marks public speech as the place where habits of character are formed. The same point appears in Paul’s warning that ‘vain babblings’ ‘increase unto more ungodliness’ and in the Buddha’s listing of idle chatter among unrighteous conduct.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Words that do not cause distress, are truthful, inoffensive, and beneficial, as well as regular recitation of the Vedic scriptures—these are declared as austerity of speech.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines disciplined speech as words that are both pleasing (priya) and beneficial (hita), among other qualities.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s priya-hita pairing mirrors the Kural’s nayan-payan pairing. Speech lacking both falls short of dharma, and the Kural adds that it removes one from goodness.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Striking structural match of the pleasing/beneficial pair; the Gita states the positive ideal rather than the harm.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns Timothy that empty, irreverent chatter has a snowballing corrupting effect.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say vain speech actively carries the speaker away from goodness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-direct parallel on idle talk as a cause of moral decline.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he who buys the amusement of speech to mislead [others] from the way of Allah without knowledge and who takes it in ridicule.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an condemns lahw al-ḥadīth, idle or diverting talk, as a means of leading people away from God’s path.
islam.tie_back: Both texts say frivolous speech pulls people away from the good path, whether the speaker’s own or other people’s.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the idea of diversion; the Qur’an focuses on misleading others, the Kural on self-corruption.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Merriment and frivolity accustom one to sexual licentiousness.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Akiva warns that light-headed, jesting talk slowly accustoms a person to serious transgression.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see frivolous words as a slope that carries a person away from virtue.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:13 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear ‘habit-formation’ parallel; Akiva names a specific sin rather than general loss of goodness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is a gossip: as one who tells that which is unseasonable … and he speaks out of season speech not worth recording, which is unreasoned, indefinite, and unconnected with good.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists idle chatter (samphappalāpa) as one of four kinds of ‘verbal conduct not in accordance with the Dhamma, unrighteous conduct’.
buddhism.tie_back: In both texts, speech ‘unconnected with good’ is a form of unrighteousness in its own right, not merely bad manners.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 41, Saleyyaka Sutta (trans. Ñanamoli Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close; idle speech is explicitly unrighteous conduct, almost the same judgment as the Kural.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “So long as he was silent, they never suspected that he was not a pigeon like themselves. But one day he was unwise enough to start chattering.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Aesop’s jackdaw disguises itself among the pigeons, gives itself away by chattering, and is driven out by both pigeons and jackdaws.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Chattering cuts the jackdaw off from both flocks, as the Kural says graceless talk cuts a person off from goodness.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, ‘The Jackdaw and the Pigeons’ (trans. V. S. Vernon Jones, 1912)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fable, not myth; the loss is social belonging rather than virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The buffoon, on the other hand, is the slave of his sense of humour, and spares neither himself nor others if he can raise a laugh, and says things none of which a man of refinement would say.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle describes the vice of excess in conversation: the buffoon’s tasteless talk departs from the mean of ready wit.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s buffoon speaks what ‘a man of refinement’ would not, which is the Kural’s பண்பில்சொல் (graceless words). Both writers call such speech a vice.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.8 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match on graceless speech as a vice of character; Aristotle’s focus is jesting, not uselessness.

kurals.tamil:
சீர்மை சிறப்பொடு நீங்கும் பயனில
நீர்மை யுடையார் சொலின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seermai sirappodu neengum payanila,
Neermai yudaiyaar solin.
kurals.meaning: If even people of good character speak empty words, their excellence and the honour it earned them both slip away.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a famous, respected captain of a sports team. If she starts saying silly, pointless things all the time, the team slowly stops looking up to her. This kural says that even good people lose their respect if they fill the air with useless words.
kurals.university: This kural turns from the habitual babbler to the virtuous person who lapses. நீர்மையுடையார் (neermaiyudaiyaar) means those who have fine nature, literally a ‘watery’ or gentle disposition. The couplet warns that they are not immune: their சீர்மை (seermai, ‘excellence, eminence’) departs together with its சிறப்பு (sirappu, ‘honour, distinction’). Solomon Pappaiah adds ‘அப்பொழுதே’ (‘at that very moment’), stressing how suddenly the loss comes. The point is that reputation is a fragile social credit, and vain talk spends it faster than virtue earns it. Ecclesiastes’ image of dead flies spoiling the perfumer’s ointment is perhaps the closest cross-cultural parallel.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the Pandavas’ Maya Sabha, Duryodhana stumbles in the illusory hall and is laughed at, and the humiliation feeds the enmity behind the dice game and the war. (Popular retellings give Draupadi a cutting jibe, but this line is not found in the critical text.)
hinduism.explanation: The Pandavas were exemplary figures, yet a moment of careless mockery by them had consequences out of all proportion.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the noble are not exempt: a few idle, mocking words can undo the standing that virtue has built.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Duryodhana’s account of the Maya Sabha; trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Weak and interpretive: the episode concerns mockery, and the famous Draupadi line is a later popular addition. Best available Hindu narrative match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour.”
christianity.explanation: A tiny contaminant spoils a costly perfume, and a little folly in the same way spoils the name of a respected sage.
christianity.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s exact thought: a person reputed for wisdom and honour loses both through a small lapse.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: the eminent lose ‘wisdom and honour’ through a little folly (the Kural specifies folly of speech).

islam.quote_or_event: “May your mother grieve your loss O Mu’adh! Are the people tossed into the Fire upon their faces, or upon their noses, except because of what their tongues have wrought.”
islam.explanation: Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal, one of the most learned Companions, is surprised to learn that people are held accountable for speech. The Prophet grasps his own tongue and says ‘Restrain this’.
islam.tie_back: Even a righteous, eminent believer is warned that the tongue can undo everything else, just as the Kural warns even people of good character.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on ‘even the virtuous are at risk from the tongue’; the stakes are eschatological rather than reputational.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Silence is fitting for the wise, and a fortiori the same is true for fools.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud cites this saying of the Sages, followed by Proverbs 17:28 (‘even a fool, when he holds his peace, is considered wise’).
judaism.tie_back: Both texts begin with the wise. The Kural warns that the good lose standing through idle talk, and the Talmud says restraint suits even the wise.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 99a (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz trans., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘even the wise’ framing, but does not describe the loss of honour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Surely, when a person is born, an axe is born in his mouth, with which he cuts himself— the fool saying a bad statement.”
buddhism.explanation: The monk Kokālika, despite having gone forth, keeps speaking against Sāriputta and Moggallāna and suffers a terrible fall.
buddhism.tie_back: A man in a revered position destroys himself with his own words, much as the Kural’s person of good character loses excellence and honour.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 3.10, Kokālika Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Kokālika’s fault is slander, not merely idle talk; the ‘self-cutting tongue’ image is the main shared element.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Thamyris “boasted that he would surpass even the Muses, daughters of aegis-bearing Jove, if they should sing against him; whereon they were angry, and maimed him. They robbed him of his divine power of song.”
greek_mythology.explanation: A gifted singer loses the very excellence he was famous for because of a vain, boastful claim.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, a person of real excellence loses that excellence and its fame through empty words.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close on ‘excellence lost through a vain word’, though the fault is hubristic boasting rather than idle chatter.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Avoid, likewise, an endeavor to excite laughter. For this is a slippery point, which may throw you into vulgar manners, and, besides, may be apt to lessen you in the esteem of your acquaintance.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus advises the aspiring philosopher that trivial, attention-seeking talk costs dignity.
philosophy.tie_back: Epictetus says it directly: frivolous talk will ‘lessen you in the esteem’ of others, even if you are a serious person. That is the Kural’s point.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close: frivolous speech reduces the esteem of a would-be good person.

kurals.tamil:
பயனில்சொல் பாராட்டு வானை மகன்எனல்
மக்கட் பதடி யெனல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Payanilsol paaraattu vaanai makanenal,
Makkat padhadi yenal.
kurals.meaning: Do not call the man who delights in showing off empty words a real man; call him the chaff among human beings.
kurals.elementary: When farmers harvest rice, the good grain is kept and the light, empty husks called chaff blow away in the wind. This kural says a person who only talks empty talk is like that chaff: they look like a person on the outside, but inside there is nothing useful.
kurals.university: Valluvar here turns from consequence to classification. பாராட்டுவான் (paaraattuvaan) means one who displays, cherishes or keeps repeating; Mu. Varadarasan glosses it as ‘saying many times’. The one who does this with பயனில்சொல் (empty words) is denied the name மகன் (makan, ‘man, human being’) and given instead மக்கட்பதடி (makkat-padhadi, ‘the chaff of humanity’). The agricultural metaphor is precise: chaff (பதர்) has the outward form of grain without its kernel, so the babbler has the form of a person without the substance that makes speech human. (One web edition prints ‘பராட்டு’ here, evidently a typo; the standard reading ‘பாராட்டு’ is followed.) The image anticipates later critiques of inauthentic ‘idle talk’, such as Heidegger’s Gerede, in which speech circulates without anyone really grasping what it is about.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrihari’s Nītiśataka says that a man without literature, music and the arts is a beast in plain sight, lacking only a tail and horns.
hinduism.explanation: The poet argues that what makes someone fully human is cultivated inner substance, not mere bodily form.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts deny full humanity to one who has the outward human form but lacks inner substance: the Kural calls him chaff, Bhartrihari a hornless beast.
hinduism.source: Bhartrihari, Nītiśataka (verse ‘sāhitya-saṅgīta-kalā-vihīnaḥ’; numbering varies by edition)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on the ‘not truly human’ rhetoric but not specific to empty speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD.”
christianity.explanation: God contrasts the empty words of false prophets (chaff) with the true word (wheat).
christianity.tie_back: Both texts use chaff as the image for words without substance, and in both the speakers of such words are judged hollow.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared chaff/grain image for empty words; Jeremiah’s target is false prophecy, not everyday idle talk.

islam.quote_or_event: “The most disliked among you to me, and the one sitting furthest from me on the Day of Judgement are the Thartharun, and the Mutashaddiqun and the Muthafaihiqun.”
islam.explanation: Tirmidhi explains that al-tharthār is ‘the one who talks a great deal’. The prophet ranks such chatterers among those furthest from him.
islam.tie_back: Both texts assign the compulsive talker the lowest rank: chaff among men, or furthest from the Prophet.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on the chatterer’s low standing; the hadith adds pomposity and arrogance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Morning sleep, midday wine, children’s talk and sitting in the assemblies of the ignorant put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas lists habits, including idle ‘children’s talk’, that drain a grown person’s life of substance.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see adult idle talk as a way of losing one’s standing as a full person.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:10 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit on idle talk hollowing out a life; no chaff image.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Sweep away the sweepings, throw away the trash, then remove the chaff: non-contemplatives who think they’re contemplatives.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the Sangha to winnow out harsh-mouthed, deluded monks who have the outward form of monks but none of the substance.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts call people chaff when they have the outward form (a man, a monk) without the inner grain.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 2.6, Dhammacariya Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking shared chaff metaphor; the target is corrupt monks generally, with harsh speech among their faults.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Echo, punished by Juno for distracting her with endless chatter, loses her own speech and can only repeat others’ last words. Pining for Narcissus, she wastes away until nothing remains but her voice.
greek_mythology.explanation: A nymph whose talk had no purpose of its own is reduced to a voice with no substance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echo’s fate turns the Kural’s ‘chaff’ into a story: a person reduced to empty sound without a kernel.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; evocative match on ‘empty voice without substance’, though Echo’s punishment is divine, not social.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heidegger describes ‘idle talk’ (Gerede) as speech that passes along what ‘one says’ without any real grasp of its subject, and he links it to an inauthentic, ‘fallen’ mode of human existence.
philosophy.explanation: For Heidegger, chatter is a symptom of losing oneself in the anonymous ‘they’ (das Man), existing as a person without being truly oneself.
philosophy.tie_back: Heidegger’s idle talker, like the Kural’s ‘chaff among men’, has the form of a speaking human but is hollow at the core.
philosophy.source: Martin Heidegger, Being and Time §35 (‘Idle Talk’)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a conceptual rather than moral-rhetorical parallel.

kurals.tamil:
நயனில சொல்லினுஞ் சொல்லுக சான்றோர்
பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Nayanila sollinum solluka saandror,
Payanila sollaamai nandru.
kurals.meaning: The worthy may, if they must, say things that are not pleasing; but it is good for them never to say things that are useless.
kurals.elementary: A good coach may sometimes say something that stings, like “You need to practise harder!” That isn’t nice to hear, but it helps. What a good coach should never do is waste the team’s time with pointless chatter. This kural says: a hard word that helps is okay, but a useless word is not.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s most philosophically daring couplet, because it ranks the two standards of speech against each other. நயனில (nayanila) is glossed by Kalaignar as ‘not sweet or pleasant’, by Pappaiah as ‘unjust’ and by Mu. Varadarasan as ‘lacking aram’. On the milder reading, Valluvar concedes that the சான்றோர் (saandror, the noble or accomplished) may speak unpleasantly, but insists that they must never speak uselessly. So usefulness (பயன்) is made the non-negotiable floor of speech, and pleasantness (நயன்) is a desirable but negotiable quality. This differs from Manu’s well-known rule against ‘disagreeable truth’, and it lines up closely with the Buddha’s criteria in the Abhaya Sutta, where beneficial but unwelcome words may be spoken at the right time and unbeneficial words never.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him say what is true, let him say what is pleasing, let him utter no disagreeable truth, and let him utter no agreeable falsehood; that is the eternal law.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu’s famous rule makes pleasantness a requirement of dharmic speech alongside truth.
hinduism.tie_back: This is an instructive contrast. Manu forbids ‘disagreeable truth’, while the Kural permits unpleasant words if they are useful. Both refuse to let empty pleasantness replace substance.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Partial and partly contrasting: Manu ranks pleasantness higher than the Kural does. Included as the closest classic Hindu statement on the same two criteria.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs values honest words that hurt over flattering ones that betray.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts accept painful words when they serve a real purpose.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the ‘unpleasant-but-useful is acceptable’ half; does not address useless speech.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asks believers for qawlan sadīdan, speech that is straight, sound and on target.
islam.tie_back: Both texts define good speech by soundness and aim rather than by softness. A straight word may not please, but it is never empty.
islam._accuracy_note: Supports ‘substance over pleasantness’ only by implication; no explicit ranking.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands tochacha (rebuke), which is unwelcome speech that is still a duty because it benefits the hearer.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts license unpleasant words when they are genuinely beneficial.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the permission for useful-but-unpleasant speech; no statement on idle speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, unbeneficial, unendearing & disagreeable to others, he does not say them. … In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, but unendearing & disagreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha sets out a grid of truth, benefit and pleasantness: unbeneficial words are never spoken, while beneficial but unpleasant words may be spoken at the right time.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s ranking: unpleasant words may be spoken if they are beneficial, and unbeneficial words are never spoken.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhaya Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: benefit is the non-negotiable criterion and pleasantness is secondary.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The blind seer Tiresias at first refuses to speak, then tells King Oedipus the painful truth that he himself is the polluter of Thebes, and is abused for it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Tiresias’ words are deeply unwelcome, but they are the only words that can save the city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tiresias shows the Kural’s concession in action: the wise may say what is unpleasant, provided it carries real weight.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good illustration of ‘unpleasant but useful’, though no statement about idle words.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I am that gadfly which God has given the state and all day long and in all places am always fastening upon you, arousing and persuading and reproaching you.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates defends his irritating questions as a benefit to Athens, like a gadfly stinging a sluggish horse.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates’ speech is famously unpleasant yet purposeful, which fits the Kural’s ideal of the sage who may sting but never babble.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the value of stinging-but-useful speech; does not address idle talk.

kurals.tamil:
அரும்பயன் ஆயும் அறிவினார் சொல்லார்
பெரும்பயன் இல்லாத சொல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arumpayan aayum arivinaar sollaar,
Perumpayan illaadha sol.
kurals.meaning: Wise people who search out rare and precious benefits never speak words that do not carry great benefit.
kurals.elementary: If you are hunting for gold, you don’t fill your bag with ordinary pebbles. Wise people are like gold-hunters with their words: they only say things that are really valuable, and they don’t waste words on things that don’t matter.
kurals.university: The couplet raises the standard. It is not enough for words to have some பயன் (benefit): the wise refuse words lacking பெரும்பயன் (perumpayan, ‘great benefit’). The rhyme of அரும்பயன் (arumpayan, ‘rare benefit’) with பெரும்பயன் binds the two halves together: those who investigate (ஆயும், aayum) rare and valuable ends apply the same selectiveness to their own speech. This describes an intellectual temperament as much as an ethical rule, since the discerning mind that weighs what is worth pursuing also weighs what is worth saying. The Upanishadic command to ‘leave off other words’, Shammai’s ‘speak little’ and Homer’s portrait of Menelaus as ‘a man of few words’ all praise the same economy of speech.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Know him alone as the Self, and leave off other words! He is the bridge of the Immortal.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad points the seeker to the one supremely valuable truth and tells him to drop all other talk.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts link devotion to the highest good with abandoning lesser speech. The Kural’s ‘rare benefit’ is here the Self.
hinduism.source: Mundaka Upanishad II.2.5 (trans. F. Max Müller, SBE 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel of ‘seek the highest, drop other words’; the Upanishad’s goal is specifically liberation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs equates wisdom with restraint in speech.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts define the wise by what they do not say.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close; Proverbs adds that many words bring sin, while the Kural stresses the standard of ‘great benefit’.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they who turn away from ill speech.”
islam.explanation: Among the defining marks of the successful believers is that they turn away from laghw, vain and pointless talk.
islam.tie_back: Both texts make refusing worthless speech a trait of those who pursue the highest good.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close; laghw is the Qur’anic counterpart of ‘payanila sol’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shammai used to say: make your [study of the] Torah a fixed practice; speak little, but do much.”
judaism.explanation: Shammai teaches that a serious person keeps words few and deeds many.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts describe the person devoted to what matters as sparing with words.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 1:15 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on economy of speech; the ‘great benefit’ criterion is implicit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is not wise because one speaks much. He who is peaceable, friendly and fearless is called wise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada separates wisdom from talkativeness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts define wisdom against mere volume of speech.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close; the Dhammapada defines wisdom by character rather than by selective speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The speech of Menelaus ran trippingly on the tongue; he did not say much, for he was a man of few words, but he spoke very clearly and to the point.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Antenor recalls the Greek embassy to Troy: Menelaus said little, but every word counted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Menelaus embodies the Kural’s ideal: few words, each carrying real weight.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close portrait of spare, weighty speech; not framed as a moral rule.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The garrulous listen to nobody, for they are always talking. And this is the first symptom of their ailment: looseness of the tongue become impotence of the ears.”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch notes that the chatterer, whom Nature gave one tongue but two ears, has stopped listening and so has stopped learning.
philosophy.tie_back: In the Kural, the wise who seek rare benefit weigh their words, and in Plutarch the babbler has stopped weighing and listening at all.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On Talkativeness (De garrulitate) 1, 502b-c (trans. W. C. Helmbold, Loeb)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Mirror-image match (describes the opposite of the wise); good on speech-versus-learning.

kurals.tamil:
பொருள்தீர்ந்த பொச்சாந்துஞ் சொல்லார் மருள்தீர்ந்த
மாசறு காட்சி யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Poruldheerndha pochchaandhum sollaar maruldheerndha,
Maasaru kaatchi yavar.
kurals.meaning: Those whose vision is spotless and free of delusion will not speak meaningless words, not even by a slip of forgetfulness.
kurals.elementary: Some people are so careful and clear-headed that even when they are tired or distracted, they don’t blurt out silly things. This kural says that people whose minds are truly clean and clear don’t say empty words even by accident.
kurals.university: The couplet balances two phrases built on தீர்ந்த (theerndha, ‘ended, freed of’). The speech is பொருள்தீர்ந்த (‘emptied of meaning’), and the speakers are மருள்தீர்ந்த (‘freed of delusion’). The symmetry suggests that meaningless words can only come from a mind that still holds some confusion. பொச்சாந்தும் (pochchaandhum, ‘even through forgetfulness/heedlessness’) raises the standard from deliberate restraint to spontaneous purity: the மாசறு காட்சியவர் (maasaru kaatchiyavar, ‘those of flawless insight’) do not need to police their tongues, because nothing empty is left in them to come out. Pochchaappu (heedlessness) later gets a chapter of its own (ch. 54, பொச்சாவாமை), which shows how central vigilance is to Valluvar’s ethics. There is a close parallel in the Buddhist portrait of the freed person whose ‘speech is calm’ and in James’s ‘perfect man’ who ‘offends not in word’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Serenity of thought, gentleness, silence, self-control, and purity of purpose—all these are declared as austerity of the mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna places mauna (silence) among the disciplines of a purified mind, not just of the tongue.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts trace restrained speech back to a purified, clear mind. Where the mind is clear, silence comes naturally.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit on the mind-speech link; the ‘not even by forgetfulness’ nuance is absent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.”
christianity.explanation: James makes perfect control of speech the mark of spiritual maturity.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts describe a rare perfection in which one does not slip in speech at all.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on ‘never slipping in word’ as the mark of the perfected; James presents it as a near-impossible ideal.

islam.quote_or_event: “A slave of Allah may utter a word without thinking whether it is right or wrong, he may slip down in the Fire as far away a distance equal to that between the east.”
islam.explanation: The hadith warns about the unconsidered word spoken carelessly.
islam.tie_back: The Kural praises the clear-minded, who do not slip even through heedlessness, and the hadith shows the danger of the heedless word they avoid.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on the ‘careless, unthinking word’ theme, expressed as a warning rather than a portrait of the sage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One who wakes up at night, or walks on the way alone and turns his heart to idle matters, behold, this man is mortally guilty.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hananiah ben Hakinai holds that even unguarded, solitary moments must not drift into idleness.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts require vigilance even in unguarded moments; the Kural says the clear-minded do not lapse even in forgetfulness.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:4 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit on vigilance in unguarded moments; concerns idle thought as much as speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Calm is his thought, calm his speech, and calm his deed, who, truly knowing, is wholly freed, perfectly tranquil and wise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada describes the arahant, freed by true knowledge, whose speech has become calm.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts describe a mind freed of delusion, from which calm, meaningful speech follows without effort.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on ‘freed mind → pure speech’; lacks the explicit ‘not even forgetfully’.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pythagorean tradition held that new disciples kept a strict silence (echemythia) for up to five years before they could speak in the school, training the mind before the tongue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The semi-legendary Pythagorean discipline treated long silence as purification that prepared a person for wise speech.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both traditions make disciplined speech the product of long mental purification, so that careless words no longer arise.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 8.10 (Pythagoras); cf. Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a semi-legendary tradition (placed here as Greek lore); a method, not a portrait of the perfected.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The world would be much happier, if men were as fully able to keep silence as they are to speak. Experience abundantly shows that men can govern anything more easily than their tongues.”
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza notes how rarely people control their speech, as evidence of how far they are from real freedom.
philosophy.tie_back: Spinoza says ordinary minds cannot govern their tongues, and the Kural says the delusion-free do so effortlessly. Both link command of speech to clarity of mind.
philosophy.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics III, Prop. 2, Scholium (trans. R. H. M. Elwes)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Complementary: Spinoza describes the common failure that the Kural’s sage has overcome.

kurals.tamil:
சொல்லுக சொல்லிற் பயனுடைய சொல்லற்க
சொல்லிற் பயனிலாச் சொல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Solluka sollir payanudaiya sollarka,
Sollir payanilaach sol.
kurals.meaning: Of all the words you could say, speak only those that are useful; of all the words you could say, never speak those that are useless.
kurals.elementary: Before you speak, ask yourself one simple question: “Will this help?” If the answer is yes, say it. If the answer is no, don’t. That’s the whole rule, and this kural says it in the simplest way possible.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with one of the most famous sound-patterns in the Kural. Forms of சொல் (sol, ‘word/speak’) occur five times: சொல்லுக (‘speak’), சொல்லில் (‘among words’, twice), சொல்லற்க (‘do not speak’) and சொல் (‘word’). The only thing that changes between the positive and negative halves is பயனுடைய / பயனிலா (‘useful / useless’). The form enacts the content: a couplet made almost entirely of the word ‘word’ shows perfect economy, with nothing wasted. Solomon Pappaiah reads பயன் as the three classical aims of life (aram, porul, inbam), which ties the rule to the whole structure of the Kural. The maxim sums up the chapter as a single test that can be applied to every utterance, much like Epictetus’s ‘speak merely what is necessary’ and the hadith ‘speak good or keep quiet’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Silence, it is said, is better than speech, if speak you must, then it is better to say the truth; if truth is to be said, it is better to say what is agreeable; and if what is agreeable is to be said, then it is better to say what is consistent with morality.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura, quoting the sage Atreya, sets out a graded ladder in which silence is the baseline and each kind of speech must improve on it.
hinduism.tie_back: In both texts, speech is only justified when it adds value that silence would not. The Kural makes benefit the test, and Vidura adds truth, agreeableness and dharma.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, section 36 (Vidura Niti) (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close structure (speak only if better than silence); the criteria differ slightly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes the hearer’s benefit (edification) the test of Christian speech.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts give the same two-part rule: speak only what builds up and withhold everything else.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: usefulness to the hearer is the criterion for all speech.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet gives a simple binary test for all speech: say what is good (khayr) or stay silent.
islam.tie_back: The hadith and the Kural state the same two-part rule: speak the beneficial and never the rest.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One who engages in idle chatter … violates a positive commandment, as it is stated: And you shall talk of them; talk of them and not of other matters.”
judaism.explanation: Rava reads Deuteronomy 6:7 (‘you shall talk of them’) as a command to fill speech with Torah and a prohibition of devarim beteilim (idle words).
judaism.tie_back: Both texts give a positive command to speak what is valuable and a matching ban on idle words.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 19b (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz trans., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in structure; ‘valuable’ is defined as Torah rather than benefit in general.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better than a thousand useless words is one useful word, hearing which one attains peace.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada measures words entirely by their usefulness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts rest on the same useful/useless contrast.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The best treasure a man can have is a sparing tongue, and the greatest pleasure, one that moves orderly; for if you speak evil, you yourself will soon be worse spoken of.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s farmer-poet counts a sparing, well-ordered tongue as a person’s best possession.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts praise economy and order in speech as the governing rule.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 719-721 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good parallel on sparing, orderly speech; Hesiod adds a warning about evil speech.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be for the most part silent, or speak merely what is necessary, and in few words.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus gives the Stoic student a rule for speech: silence by default, with only necessary words.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts lay down a rule of speech governed by necessity and usefulness.
